steps.tx: An **avascular necrosis** of the femoral head represents cellular death of bone and marrow elements resulting from compromised microvascular blood supply. The anterosuperior weight-bearing dome is most vulnerable because it relies on terminal retinacular branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery. Major non-traumatic etiologies encompass chronic corticosteroid therapy, heavy alcohol consumption, sickle cell disease, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
steps.say: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head is bone infarction caused by interrupted blood supply. The upper weight-bearing part of the head is most vulnerable because it depends on terminal branches of the medial femoral circumflex artery. High-dose steroids, alcohol abuse, sickle cell disease, and lupus are the classic non-traumatic causes.

vis.title: Etiological Risk Factors
rows: Displaced neck femur or hip dislocation

steps.tx: The widely adopted **Ficat-Arlet classification** stages disease progression based on clinical symptoms, plain radiographs, and magnetic resonance imaging. Stage 0 is preclinical and preradiographic. Stage I features normal radiographs but positive magnetic resonance imaging. Stage II shows patchy sclerosis and osteopenia with a preserved spherical contour. Stage III demonstrates subchondral fracture with articular flattening. Stage IV exhibits secondary osteoarthritis.
steps.say: Ficat and Arlet staged avascular necrosis from zero to four. Stage zero is silent with normal tests. Stage one has normal X-rays but abnormal magnetic resonance imaging. Stage two shows patchy sclerosis on X-ray, but the head remains round. Stage three shows subchondral collapse, seen as the crescent sign. Stage four is secondary osteoarthritis.

steps.tx: In Stage III disease, plain radiographs demonstrate the pathognomonic **crescent sign**, visualized best on the frog-leg lateral pelvic projection. The crescent represents a thin, curved radiolucent subchondral fracture line separating necrotic cancellous bone from overlying intact articular cartilage. Its appearance signals impending structural collapse of the weight-bearing dome and marks the critical transition where joint-preserving procedures fail.
steps.say: The crescent sign on a frog-leg lateral X-ray confirms stage three. It is a curved dark sliver of air or fluid right beneath the joint cartilage, indicating that the dead bone underneath has fractured. Once you see the crescent sign, the femoral head is collapsing, and joint-preserving operations will no longer work.

left.title: Crescent Sign Pathomechanics
points: Separates articular cartilage from dead bone
Best seen on frog-leg lateral X-ray

right.title: Double-Line Sign on MRI
points: Diagnostic in Stage I and II pre-collapse

steps.tx: In pre-collapse stages (Ficat I and II), surgical **core decompression** reduces elevated intraosseous compartmental pressure, venting congested venous sinusoids to stimulate neovascularization. Drilling an eight-millimeter channel or multiple small percutaneous tracks into the necrotic anterosuperior lesion, often combined with autologous bone marrow aspirate concentrate (BMAC), halts progression and preserves native joint architecture in up to eighty percent of cases.
steps.say: In stage one and two before bone collapses, perform core decompression. Drilling a tunnel into the dead segment relieves trapped marrow pressure and allows new blood vessels to sprout into the dead bone. Adding bone marrow stem cells from the iliac crest boosts bone regeneration and prevents the hip from collapsing in eighty percent of patients.

left.title: Core Decompression Alone
points: 8 mm drill channel into necrotic zone

right.title: Biologically Augmented Decompression
points: Delivers mesenchymal stem cells and VEGF
Superior survivorship in Ficat II disease

steps.tx: Once structural collapse occurs in Ficat Stages III and IV, joint-preserving procedures are futile, and **total hip arthroplasty** becomes the definitive gold-standard solution. Cementless porous-coated acetabular cups and femoral stems provide biologic osseous ingrowth. Modern bearing surfaces such as ceramic-on-ceramic or ceramic-on-cross-linked polyethylene deliver exceptional long-term survivorship exceeding ninety percent at twenty years, even in young active patients.
steps.say: Once the femoral head has collapsed into stage three or four, total hip arthroplasty is the only reliable cure. A cementless ceramic-on-polyethylene or ceramic-on-ceramic replacement eliminates pain and restores full function, achieving over ninety percent implant survival at twenty years.

quiz.q: Which radiographic sign in Ficat Stage III femoral avascular necrosis signifies subchondral bone fracture?
options: Crescent sign on frog-leg lateral radiograph
Terry Thomas sign on anteroposterior view
Codman triangle at the femoral neck
quiz.explain: The crescent sign, best seen on frog-leg lateral views, represents a subchondral fracture between the necrotic bone and overlying cartilage in Ficat Stage III.

quiz.q: What is the primary objective of core decompression in early-stage (Ficat I and II) avascular necrosis?
options: Relieving elevated intraosseous marrow pressure and stimulating neovascularization
Excising the dead bone and replacing it with a titanium endoprosthesis
Realigning the femoral neck into thirty degrees of anatomical valgus
Inducing chemical arthrodesis across the hip articulation
quiz.explain: Core decompression decreases elevated intraosseous compartmental pressure and creates a channel for creeping substitution and neovascular ingrowth into the necrotic bone.
